The Southern African anchovy Engraulis capensis is a pelagic teleost that dominates the productive upwelling system of the Benguela Current. Field surveys indicate that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from fertilised ova after approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days] at a water temperature of 13.7 °C [T = 13.7 °C], a period consistent with the rapid embryogenesis documented in other Engraulidae from similar thermal regimes. The dry weight at birth for these lecithotrophic prolarvae is estimated at 0.3 milligrams [Wwb = 0.3 milligrams], reflecting the modest endogenous yolk reserves packaged into the transparent, pelagic egg. This initial mass, while small, supports the non-feeding larva through the critical period of yolk absorption and the onset of exogenous feeding. The mouth-gape opening and retinal differentiation that enable first prey capture occur during the late yolk-sac stage, after which the actively growing ichthyoplankton enters the postflexion phase and begins its pelagic larval trajectory toward juvenile recruitment.

Reproductive output in Engraulis capensis is characterised by a high fecundity that is typical of small, short-lived clupeoids. Published estimates of relative annual fecundity in the congeneric European anchovy Engraulis encrasicolus range from 9000 to 11 000 oocytes per gram of somatic mass, and similar values are assumed for the Southern African species. In practical terms, a sexually mature female with a standard length at puberty of 9.5 cm [Lp = 9.5 cm] produces approximately 10,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 10,000 eggs per spawning event] with about 30 spawning events per year [F_R_i = about 30 spawning events per year] when water temperatures remain near 13.7 °C [T = 13.7 °C], although this maximum daily reproductive rate is observed only during the peak of the protracted spawning season. The capacity for repeated batch spawning over several months allows a single adult female to release tens of thousands of oocytes annually, a strategy that buffers recruitment against the high interannual variability in prey availability and advective losses characteristic of the Benguela ecosystem. The onset of vitellogenesis and subsequent first spawning event occur shortly after the individual reaches the critical length that signals the completion of somatic growth.

Adult body size in Engraulis capensis is relatively modest compared to other pelagic teleosts in the southern Atlantic. The ultimate standard length attained by fully grown individuals is approximately 17 cm [Li = approximately 17 cm], a value derived from extensive length-frequency distributions sampled during research trawl surveys conducted by the South African Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for a fish of this length is 50.5 grams [Wwi = 50.5 grams], based on length-weight regressions developed specifically for this species using specimens collected across the continental shelf between Cape Point and the Orange River. These morphometric measurements place Engraulis capensis among the smaller members of the genus Engraulis, somewhat below the maximum sizes reported for Engraulis mordax from the California Current system. The relationship between standard length and wet weight describes a robust, fusiform body plan that is energetically efficient for sustained filter feeding on dense aggregations of copepods and euphausiids that characterise the cold, nutrient-rich waters of the Benguela.

The standard length at which Engraulis capensis attains puberty has been determined through histological examination of gonadal development in field-collected individuals. Sexual maturation, marked by the onset of spermatogenesis in males and the commencement of vitellogenesis in females, is consistently observed at a standard length of 9.5 cm [Lp = 9.5 cm]. At this size, the reproductively viable adults are capable of participating in the main spawning aggregations that form during the austral spring and summer months. The allocation of resources toward gonad development rather than continued somatic growth becomes apparent at this physiological transition, after which the proportion of body mass devoted to ovarian tissue increases markedly. This standard length at first puberty corresponds to an age of approximately 6 to 8 months under the prevailing thermal conditions in the southern Benguela, a rapid maturation strategy that enables populations to recover quickly from environmental perturbations such as reduced upwelling or low prey densities that can cause recruitment failures in consecutive years.

Maximum longevity in Engraulis capensis is constrained by the high metabolic demands of its active, pelagic lifestyle and by intense predation pressure from larger fish, seabirds, and marine mammals. The lifespan reported for this species is approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] under the thermal conditions of its natural habitat at 13.7 °C [T = 13.7 °C], a value consistent with the known longevity of the closely related European anchovy Engraulis encrasicolus. This relatively short lifespan places Engraulis capensis at the short-lived end of the teleost life-history continuum, a position that aligns with its small adult body size and high fecundity. The species is effectively semelparous in the sense that most individuals die soon after their first or second spawning season, although a small proportion of the population may survive to spawn for a third year. Reproductive senescence has not been formally documented in this species, likely because extrinsic mortality factors typically remove individuals before any age-related decline in physiological function can become apparent within the wild population.
